Lesson 0009 · Silmulator · from issue #18, commit 58b7e2d

ADC Transfer Functions: the Reference as the Unit of Measure

Why this matters: an ADC code is not a voltage — it is a ratio against the selected reference. Until commit 58b7e2d the MSP430 model hardcoded 3.3 V, so every reference-scaling bug in user code was invisible to SIL tests.

Sections:
☐ 1. A code is a ratio
☐ 2. The transfer function
☐ 3. The fix (58b7e2d)
☐ 4. The fixed reference set
☐ 5. Full scale & LSB
☐ 6. Why SIL cares
☐ 7. Misconceptions
☐ 8. Quiz
☐ 9. Scenarios

1. An ADC Code Is a Ratio, Not a Voltage

The single most important idea in this lesson: the number an ADC returns has no voltage unit attached to it. A 12-bit ADC answers exactly one question — "what fraction of the reference span is the input sitting at?" — quantised into 4096 steps.

The reference voltage is the unit of measure. Reading code 2047 tells you the input is at roughly half the reference — and nothing more. Half of what depends entirely on which reference was selected when the conversion ran:

Code returnedSelected reference (VR+)Actual input voltage
20471.2 V (internal VREF)≈ 0.60 V
20472.5 V (internal VREF2.5)≈ 1.25 V
20473.3 V (AVCC)≈ 1.65 V

Same code, three different physical voltages. Conversely, the same input voltage produces different codes under different references:

InputReference (VR+)Code (12-bit)Meaning
1.2 V1.2 V (VREF)4095Full scale — input equals the reference
1.2 V2.0 V (VREF2.0)245760% of span
1.2 V2.5 V (VREF2.5)196548% of span
1.2 V3.3 V (AVCC)1489≈36% of span
💡 The mental model
Think of the reference as a ruler. The ADC reports "the input reaches the 1489th tick mark of my 4096-tick ruler." If you swap in a shorter ruler (a smaller reference), the same input reaches a higher tick mark. The tick number is meaningless until you know which ruler was used.

2. The Transfer Function — SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13

TI's MSP430FR58xx/59xx family user's guide (SLAU367P) defines the ADC12_B conversion result in §34.2.1, Equation 13:

NADC  =  4095  ×  Vin − VR− VR+ − VR− 4095 = full-scale code for 12-bit mode; more generally FS = 2resolution − 1
  • Vin — the analog input voltage on the selected channel.
  • VR+ — the positive reference: the voltage that maps to full scale. Selected by ADC12VRSEL.
  • VR− — the negative reference: the voltage that maps to code 0. In Silmulator's model it is fixed at AVSS (0 V), so the equation simplifies to N = FS × Vin / VR+.
  • FS — the full-scale code: 4095 (12-bit), 1023 (10-bit), or 255 (8-bit), matching ADC12RES.

Worked example 1 — the probe case: 1.2 V input against the 1.2-V VREF

N = 4095 × (1.2 − 0) / (1.2 − 0)
  = 4095 × 1.0
  = 4095   # full scale — the input IS the reference

Worked example 2 — the same 1.2 V input against AVCC = 3.3 V

N = 4095 × (1.2 − 0) / (3.3 − 0)
  = 4095 × 0.36363…
  = 1489.09  →  int()  →  1489

Identical input, two references, codes of 4095 vs 1489. This exact pair is the audit probe (adc_ignores_reference) that exposed the bug: the old model returned 1489 regardless of the selected reference.

Worked example 3 — recovering volts from a code

Firmware and test scripts invert the transfer function to get volts back:

Vin ≈ N / FS × (VR+ − VR−) + VR−
     = 1489 / 4095 × 3.3
     = 1.19993 V   # ~1.2 V recovered — but ONLY if you divide by the SAME reference
⚠ Truncation, not rounding
Silmulator's nominal profile uses int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) — Python's int() truncates toward zero. An ideal result of 2047.5 becomes 2047, not 2048. Keep this in mind when predicting exact codes in the drill.

3. The Fix — What Commit 58b7e2d Actually Changed

Issue #18 came out of the MSP430 compliance audit (docs/audits/msp430-compliance-report.md). Two ADC families were NON_COMPLIANT for the same root cause: the model ignored the reference.

Before: a hardcoded 3.3 in the conversion path

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — BEFORE 58b7e2d
def _adc_ch_raw(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ac: ADCChannel) -> str:
    return str(self.faults.adc_code(ac.value, 3.3, ac.resolution))
                                              # ↑ VR+ frozen at 3.3 V forever

And ADC:REFERENCE stored any string without complaint — ADC:REFERENCE BANANA succeeded, and the stored value was never read by the conversion code. Two independent defects: no validation and no effect.

After: VR+ is resolved from the selected reference at conversion time

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — AFTER 58b7e2d
def _adc_ch_raw(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ac: ADCChannel) -> str:
    return str(self.faults.adc_code(ac.value, self._adc_reference_voltage(), ac.resolution))

def _adc_reference_voltage(self) -> float:
    """VR+ in volts for the selected ADC reference (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13).

    VR- is AVSS (0 V) in this model — the simulator does not expose the
    VR- half of ADC12VRSEL's combinations, only which source drives VR+.
    """
    ref = self.adc[0].reference
    if ref == "AVCC":
        return self.clock.vcc          # reads CPU:VCC live — not a snapshot
    if ref == "VEREF":
        return self._veref_v           # the external VeREF+ pin voltage
    return ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V.get(ref, self.clock.vcc)  # REF_A outputs

The new module-level reference table

# REF_A's three internal reference outputs (SLAU367P §33.3.1, REFVSEL field).
# Bare "VREF" maps to REFVSEL's reset value (00b = 1.2 V).
ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V: Dict[str, float] = {
    "VREF":    1.2,
    "VREF1.2": 1.2,
    "VREF2.0": 2.0,
    "VREF2.5": 2.5,
}

# The fixed set ADC:REFERENCE accepts: AVCC (tracks CPU:VCC), REF_A's internal
# outputs, and VEREF (the external VeREF+ pin). Anything else has no
# ADC12VRSEL encoding and is rejected with -224.
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V))

Validation in the SCPI handler

def _adc_ref(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    if cmd.is_query:
        return self.adc[0].reference
    if cmd.params:
        ref = cmd.params[0].upper()
        if ref not in VALID_ADC_REFERENCES:
            raise ScpiError(-224, f"Illegal ADC reference: {ref}")
        if ref == "VEREF" and len(cmd.params) > 1:
            try:
                self._veref_v = float(cmd.params[1])
            except ValueError:
                raise ScpiError(-104, f"Invalid VEREF voltage: {cmd.params[1]}")
        for ch in self.adc.values():
            ch.reference = ref     # one reference for all channels (single-VR+ model)
    return ""

Tests flipped from expected-failure to passing

The two audit-derived tests dropped their @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) decorators — the code now does what SLAU367P says:

# tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — AFTER 58b7e2d (xfail decorators removed)
def test_reference_out_of_range_rejected(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §34.2.4 (ADC12VRSEL), §33 (REF_A): the reference is selected
    # from a fixed set (AVCC, 1.2/2.0/2.5-V REF, external) — not free-form.
    mcu.process("ADC:REFERENCE BANANA")
    assert errors(mcu) == 1

def test_raw_respects_selected_reference(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13: with VR+ = 1.2-V VREF, a 1.2-V input is full scale.
    mcu.process("ADC:REFERENCE VREF")
    mcu.inject_adc(0, 1.2)
    assert int(mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?")) == 4095

Compliance moved from 19.8% → 22.8%: ADC:CHANNELn:RAW, ADC:CHn:RAW, and ADC:REFERENCE all flipped NON_COMPLIANT → COMPLIANT. (ADC:CONVERT now scales correctly too but stays NON_COMPLIANT for unrelated reasons: it runs without ADC12ENC and returns '0' for nonexistent channels.)

📌 One more detail: *RST
The new VeREF+ pin state self._veref_v is reset to 1.2 in the *RST handler, alongside all other peripheral state. Any new device state you add must be reset there too — that's the *RST contract.

4. Why References Are a Fixed Hardware Set (and -224 for Everything Else)

On a real MSP430FR5994 you cannot ask for a "1.8 V reference". The positive reference is selected by ADC12VRSEL — a 4-bit field in ADC12MCTLx (SLAU367P §34.2.4) whose encodings pick which physical voltage source drives VR+ and VR−. A register field with a finite set of encodings is the hardware truth the simulator must mirror.

The sources Silmulator models

SCPI tokenPhysical sourceVR+ value
AVCCThe analog supply railWhatever CPU:VCC is — read live at conversion time (default 3.3 V)
VREFREF_A internal reference, REFVSEL reset default (00b)1.2 V
VREF1.2REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 00b1.2 V
VREF2.0REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 01b2.0 V
VREF2.5REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 10b2.5 V
VEREFThe external VeREF+ pin (board-supplied)Whatever the test sets, e.g. ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 (default 1.2 V)

Three different kinds of reference source

  • AVCC — the supply itself. Cheap and always available, but it moves with the supply: brown-outs, battery droop, and regulator tolerance all show up as measurement error. Silmulator models this honestly: _adc_reference_voltage() reads self.clock.vcc at every conversion, so CPU:VCC 3.0 immediately rescales all subsequent conversions.
  • REF_A internal outputs — the FR5994's shared reference module (SLAU367P §33) generates precise 1.2 / 2.0 / 2.5 V from an internal bandgap, independent of the supply. This is what you use when the measurement must be in absolute volts.
  • VeREF+ — an external pin (SLASE54D Table 7-1) for boards that provide their own precision reference IC. Its voltage is whatever the board designer wired up — which is why Silmulator lets the test declare it: ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048.

Why -224 specifically?

SCPI error -224, "Illegal parameter value" is the standard code for "the parameter is the right type but not one of the permitted values." The token BANANA (or 1.8, or 3V3) parses fine as a string — it just has no ADC12VRSEL encoding. Compare:

  • ADC:REFERENCE BANANA → -224 — not in the value set. The stored reference is left unchanged (still the AVCC default).
  • ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,notanumber → -104, "Data type error" — the reference token is valid, but the second parameter must be numeric.
  • ADC:RESOLUTION 9 → -224 — the sibling precedent: ADC12RES only encodes 8/10/12 bits, so 9 is rejected the same way.
💡 The design rule
When a SCPI parameter mirrors a hardware register field, the accepted value set is exactly the register's encodings — no more, no less. Free-form acceptance is how a simulator ends up blessing configurations that no silicon can express.

5. Full Scale, Clipping, and the LSB

Clipping: inputs above VR+ saturate

faults.adc_code() clamps the result to [0, max_code]. An input above the reference doesn't wrap or error — it pegs at full scale, exactly like real hardware:

# msp430_faults.py — nominal profile
max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1            # 4095 / 1023 / 255
code = int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)
return max(0, min(max_code, code))          # ← the clamp
Inject 2.5 V, reference VREF2.0:
N = 4095 × 2.5 / 2.0 = 5118.75  →  clamped  →  4095

Reading 4095 therefore means "at or above the reference" — the true voltage is unrecoverable. A real design leaves headroom; a SIL test can now verify that firmware treats 4095 as saturation, not as a valid measurement.

The LSB: what one code step is worth

One least-significant-bit step corresponds to (VR+ − VR−) / FS volts. The reference sets not just the range but the granularity:

ReferenceRange1 LSB (12-bit)Trade-off
VREF 1.2 V0 – 1.2 V≈ 293 µVFinest resolution, smallest range
VREF2.00 – 2.0 V≈ 488 µV
VREF2.50 – 2.5 V≈ 611 µV
AVCC 3.3 V0 – 3.3 V≈ 806 µVWidest range, coarsest steps, supply-dependent

This is why real firmware picks the smallest reference that still covers the signal: a 0–1 V sensor read against the 1.2-V VREF uses ~83% of the code space; against AVCC it uses only ~30%, throwing away 1.4 bits of effective resolution.

Resolution interacts the same way

ADC:RESOLUTION 8 changes FS to 255: injecting 3.3 V against AVCC 3.3 gives int(3.3/3.3 × 255) = 255 — the existing edge-case test. Reference and resolution are the two knobs of the same equation.

Ratiometric measurement: when AVCC is the right answer

If the sensor itself is powered from AVCC (a potentiometer, a resistive bridge), its output is already a fraction of AVCC. Converting it against AVCC makes the supply cancel out of the equation:

N = FS × k · AVCCAVCC = FS × k the code depends only on the sensor's fraction k — supply drift disappears

This is ratiometric measurement, and it is the reason "AVCC" exists as a reference choice at all. Silmulator's live clock.vcc read makes this testable: drop CPU:VCC and a ratiometric setup's code stays put, while an absolute-reference setup's code shifts.

6. Why This Matters for SIL Testing

Silmulator's purpose is to catch embedded-firmware bugs before hardware exists. The hardcoded 3.3 V broke that promise in a very specific way — it made the simulator agree with buggy firmware.

The bug class that was invisible

Consider firmware that configures the 2.5-V internal reference but converts codes to volts with the wrong constant:

/* firmware under test — BUG: reference is 2.5 V, math assumes 3.3 V */
float read_battery_volts(void) {
    select_reference(REF_2V5);            /* ADC12VRSEL = internal 2.5 V   */
    uint16_t raw = adc_convert(CH0);
    return raw / 4095.0f * 3.3f;          /* ← wrong unit of measure!      */
}
  • Old model: the simulated ADC also divided by 3.3, so raw/4095×3.3 round-tripped perfectly. The test passed. The bug shipped.
  • New model: injecting 1.5 V gives raw = int(1.5/2.5×4095) = 2457; the firmware computes 2457/4095×3.3 = 1.98 V. The SIL test's assertion ≈1.5 V fails — the mis-scaling is caught in simulation, exactly where it should be.

What else becomes testable

  • Reference-selection typos: firmware SCPI-driving a bad token now queues -224 instead of silently "working".
  • Supply-droop behaviour: CPU:VCC 3.0 rescales AVCC-referenced conversions live (1.2 V now reads 1638 instead of 1489) — brown-out compensation logic can be exercised.
  • Saturation handling: over-range inputs peg at 4095; firmware that treats 4095 as a real reading can be flagged.
  • Board-specific references: ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 models a precision external reference IC without any Python changes.
⚠ The general lesson
A simulator defect is worse than a missing feature. A missing feature fails loudly; a wrong constant makes the simulator and the buggy firmware wrong in the same direction, and every test between them passes. That is why the compliance audit probes behaviour (adc_ignores_reference) rather than trusting the command to exist.

7. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"Code 4095 means 3.3 V" Code 4095 means Vin ≥ VR+, whatever VR+ currently is. Under VREF it means ≥1.2 V; it can also mean the input is clipping far above the reference.
Reference voltage vs. supply voltage AVCC can serve as the reference, but they are distinct roles. The supply powers the chip; the reference defines the conversion's unit of measure. Only when ADC12VRSEL selects AVCC do they coincide — and then supply noise becomes measurement noise.
VREF vs VREF2.5 Bare VREF is not "some generic reference" — it maps to REFVSEL's reset value, 00b = 1.2 V. VREF1.2/2.0/2.5 select explicitly. Sending ADC:REFERENCE VREF and expecting 2.5-V scaling is a real trap.
ADC:CHANNELn:VALUE? vs :RAW? VALUE? returns the injected voltage in volts — test-harness introspection, no real-register counterpart (UNDOCUMENTED in the audit). RAW? is the modelled register read: a code, scaled by the reference. Only RAW goes through the transfer function.
-224 vs -104 -224 "Illegal parameter value": right type, not in the permitted set (ADC:REFERENCE BANANA). -104 "Data type error": wrong type entirely (ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,notanumber — the voltage must parse as a float).
Full-scale code vs full-scale voltage The full-scale code is fixed by resolution (4095 at 12-bit). The full-scale voltage is whatever reference you selected. Changing the reference moves the voltage that produces 4095; it never changes 4095 itself.

8. Quiz

Q1. With ADC:REFERENCE VREF2.0 selected and 1.0 V injected on channel 3, what does ADC:CHANNEL3:RAW? return in 12-bit mode?

  • 2047
  • 2048
  • 1241
  • 4095

Q2. A test sends ADC:REFERENCE 1.8 hoping for a 1.8-V reference. What happens?

  • The reference is set to 1.8 V and conversions scale accordingly
  • SCPI error -224 is queued and the previously selected reference is unchanged
  • SCPI error -104 is queued
  • It rounds to the nearest available reference (VREF2.0)

Q3. Why does _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc for AVCC instead of the constant 3.3?

  • Pure style — 3.3 would work identically but constants are discouraged
  • AVCC is the live supply rail — CPU:VCC 3.0 must rescale subsequent conversions, as on real hardware
  • Because VEREF shares the same storage variable
  • Because the internal 1.2/2.0/2.5-V references also scale with VCC

Q4. With ADC:REFERENCE VREF2.0 selected, 2.5 V is injected. What does a 12-bit RAW read return, and why?

  • SCPI error -222 (data out of range)
  • 4095 — the ideal 5118 is clamped to full scale (clipping)
  • 1022 — the result wraps modulo 4096
  • 3103

Q5. Before commit 58b7e2d, a SIL test of firmware that selected the 2.5-V reference but converted codes with raw/4095×3.3 would pass. Why?

  • Simulator and firmware were both wrong by the same 3.3-V factor, so the errors cancelled
  • The old model rejected the 2.5-V reference so the firmware fell back to AVCC
  • The old model only supported 8-bit conversions
  • Voltage injection was broken before the commit

9. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: Your board has a precision 2.048-V reference IC wired to the VeREF+ pin. Write the SCPI sequence to configure the simulated MSP430 to match, inject 1.024 V on channel 2, and predict the 12-bit RAW result. What error would you get if you typo'd the voltage as 2.O48 (letter O)?
Show answer 
ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048     ← selects the external pin AND sets its voltage
ADC:CHANNEL2:INJECT 1.024
ADC:CHANNEL2:RAW?             → int(1.024 / 2.048 × 4095) = int(2047.5) = 2047

Exactly half the reference → half of full scale (truncated from 2047.5). With ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.O48, the token VEREF is valid but float("2.O48") raises ValueError, so the handler queues -104, "Invalid VEREF voltage: 2.O48" — a data-type error, not -224. The previously stored _veref_v is untouched. Also remember *RST resets _veref_v to 1.2, so the sequence must run after any reset.

Scenario B: A teammate reports "the ADC model is broken — I inject 1.2 V and RAW? returns 4095, but 1.2/3.3×4095 should be 1489." What do you check first, and what do you tell them?
Show answer

Check the selected reference: ADC:REFERENCE?. Almost certainly it returns VREF — someone (or a previous test, since the reference persists until *RST) selected the internal 1.2-V reference. Under VR+ = 1.2 V, a 1.2-V input is full scale: N = 4095 × 1.2/1.2 = 4095. This is the exact behaviour test_raw_respects_selected_reference asserts.

The teammate's formula smuggles in the assumption that 3.3 V is the unit of measure. The 1489 figure is only correct when AVCC (at its 3.3-V default) is selected. Their expectation is the pre-58b7e2d bug — the model used to behave that way, and it was NON_COMPLIANT. The fix: state expected codes as a function of the selected reference, or explicitly select ADC:REFERENCE AVCC at test setup.

Scenario C: You're writing a SIL test for battery-monitoring firmware that must keep working as the supply sags from 3.3 V to 3.0 V. The firmware measures a fixed 1.2-V bandgap-derived signal using AVCC as the reference and infers the supply from the code. Using only SCPI, how do you simulate the sag and what codes should the test expect at each supply level?
Show answer 
ADC:REFERENCE AVCC            ← unit of measure = the live supply
ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.2       ← the fixed signal being measured

CPU:VCC 3.3
ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?             → int(1.2/3.3 × 4095) = 1489

CPU:VCC 3.0                   ← simulate the sag
ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?             → int(1.2/3.0 × 4095) = 1638

Because _adc_reference_voltage() reads clock.vcc live, no re-arming is needed — the very next conversion uses the new supply. The trick the firmware exploits is the transfer function in reverse: the input is fixed, so a rising code means a falling reference. AVCC ≈ 4095 × 1.2 / N, so N = 1638 → AVCC ≈ 3.0 V. This measure-the-ruler-with-a-known-stick technique is only testable because the model stopped hardcoding 3.3 V.

1	# Silmulator — Glossary
2	
3	Terms the learner has demonstrably grasped are added here.
4	
5	| Term | Definition |
6	|------|------------|
7	| ConnectionPort | A `QGraphicsEllipseItem` child of a block that holds `port_id`, `parent_block`, and `connected_to` (the peer port, or None). Coloured blue when free, green when connected. |
8	| WireItem | A `QGraphicsLineItem` in the scene (not a child of any block) that draws a gold line between two ConnectionPorts. ZValue = -1 so blocks render above it. |
9	| x_frac / y_frac | Fractional coordinates (0.0–1.0) passed to `add_port()` that are multiplied by the block's BLOCK_WIDTH / BLOCK_HEIGHT to position a port in local coordinates. |
10	| hardware_docs/ | The folder in the repo where vendor PDFs, SCPI command tables, and notes are stored. Not auto-parsed; feeds the custom-block authoring workflow. |
11	| custom block spec | A JSON file in `silmulator/custom_blocks/` that declares a block's name, colour, port layout, and SCPI command map. Loaded at startup by `discover_specs()`. |
12	| SIL | Software-in-the-Loop: both the controller logic and the instruments are simulated in software. No real hardware. |
13	| HIL | Hardware-in-the-Loop: the real embedded controller runs in real time; only the instruments/plant are simulated. |
14	| CIL | Code-in-the-Loop: actual source files are the artifact under test; SCPI calls extracted from them are replayed against simulated instruments. The Code Input block enables this. |
15	| SCPI | Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (IEEE 488.2). A tree-structured text command language used by lab instruments and simulated here. |
16	| reference voltage | The voltage pair (VR+/VR−) an ADC compares its input against — the conversion's unit of measure. In the MSP430 model, `_adc_reference_voltage()` resolves VR+ from the selected `ADC:REFERENCE` (AVCC live via `clock.vcc`, REF_A outputs, or VeREF+); VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V). |
17	| full-scale code | The maximum ADC output, 2^resolution − 1 (4095/1023/255). Produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage. Clamped in `FaultState.adc_code()`. |
18	| transfer function | The input→code mapping NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−)/(VR+ − VR−) (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13). An ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage. Implemented as `int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)`, clamped. |
19	| LSB voltage | The input-voltage width of one code step: (VR+ − VR−)/FS. ≈293 µV under the 1.2-V VREF vs ≈806 µV under 3.3-V AVCC at 12 bits — the reference sets granularity as well as range. |
20	| ADC12VRSEL | The 4-bit ADC12MCTLx field (SLAU367P §34.2.4) selecting which physical sources drive VR+/VR−. A finite register encoding — mirrored by `VALID_ADC_REFERENCES`, which is why `ADC:REFERENCE BANANA` is rejected with SCPI -224. |
21	| REF_A | The FR5994's shared internal reference module (SLAU367P §33): bandgap-derived 1.2/2.0/2.5-V outputs selected by REFVSEL (reset default 00b = 1.2 V). Modelled by the `ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V` dict; bare `VREF` maps to the reset default. |
22	| VeREF+ | The external positive-reference pin (SLASE54D Table 7-1) — board-supplied, no defined reset state. Modelled as `_veref_v`, set via `ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,<v>` (non-numeric voltage → SCPI -104), reset to 1.2 by `*RST`. |
23	| ratiometric measurement | Referencing the ADC to the same source that powers the sensor so the supply cancels: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k. The reason AVCC exists as a reference choice; testable because AVCC reads `clock.vcc` live at conversion time. |
24	| register width | The number of physical flip-flops in a register, fixing its representable values at 0 … 2^width − 1. TAxR/TAxCCRn are 16-bit; writes outside 0–0xFFFF are rejected with SCPI -222 (`_timer_count`, `_timer_cc_val`). Python ints are unbounded, so the model must enforce width explicitly. |
25	| encoding | The finite mapping from a register field's bit patterns to behaviours — an n-bit field reaches at most 2^n values. The timer divider is ID (2 bits) × TAIDEX (3 bits), max /64; /128 has no encoding and draws -224. Width bounds magnitude; encoding bounds meaning. |
26	| reachable state space | The set of states real hardware can occupy — the closure of all field encodings. A simulator's accepted inputs must stay inside it: accepting an unreachable state (the old /128) silently voids every downstream SIL result. The accepted set may be a documented *subset* (the power-of-two dividers). |
27	| write masking | Truncating an over-width write to the register width (`value & 0xFFFF`) instead of refusing it — what a 16-bit bus does physically. Silmulator rejects with -222 instead; `test_count_over_16bit_rejected_or_masked` blesses either policy, forbidding only verbatim storage. |
28	| TAIDEX | The 3-bit input divider expansion field in TAxEX0 (÷1…8), cascaded after ID (÷1/2/4/8) in TAxCTL. Effective divider = ID × TAIDEX product: 20 reachable values, max 8×8 = /64 — why `TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128` is impossible and rejected. |
29	| CAP bit | The per-CC-unit mode bit in TAxCCTLn: compare (CCRn holds a written value) vs capture (an edge latches the count into CCRn). Stored state since a20fbb1 (`cc_mode` dict, -224 validation); capture *events* are out of scope — time does not pass. |
30	| register aliasing | Two interface names denoting one physical register, modeled as delegation to a single store. PERIOD IS TAxCCR0 (SLAU367P §25.2.3.1): `_timer_period` is `return self._timer_cc_val(cmd, ts, 0)` — the old independent `period` field was the double-store bug class. |
31	| stored-state modeling | Simulating a device as a validated state machine with no autonomous dynamics: registers hold what was written; counting, latching, and interrupts never happen because time does not pass. Model configuration fully, document dynamics as out of scope — never fake them. |
32	| clock tree | The routing structure sources → muxes → dividers → consumers: a clock's frequency is a path property (selected source ÷ divider), never a stored number. Since 701853d, `_clk_*_freq` walks it via `_clock_source_frequency(source)/div` instead of hardwiring DCO/LFXT. |
33	| SELM/SELS/SELA | The CSCTL2 source-select mux fields (SLAU367P §3.3.2). SELM/SELS share the six-entry menu {LFXT, VLO, LFMODCLK, DCO, MODCLK, HFXT}; SELA offers only {LFXT, VLO, LFMODCLK}. Mirrored by two frozensets; unencodable tokens (REFO, BANANA) draw SCPI -224. |
34	| DIVM/DIVS/DIVA | The CSCTL3 clock dividers (SLAU367P §3.3.3): 3-bit fields encoding powers of two /1–/32 only. `VALID_CLOCK_DIVIDERS = {1,2,4,8,16,32}`; /64 has no encoding and is rejected with -222, leaving prior state unchanged. |
35	| VLO | The internal very-low-power oscillator: ~9.4 kHz typical, uncalibrated, no configuration register (SLAU367P §3.2.6). Modeled as the constant `VLO_FREQUENCY_HZ = 9400.0` — a valid source for all three clocks, ~3.49× slower than LFXT's 32768 Hz. |
36	| MODCLK | The internal ~4.8-MHz module oscillator (SLAU367P §3.2.5), fixed-rate with no register: `MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ = 4.8e6`. A documented MCLK/SMCLK source (SELM encoding 4) that the pre-701853d model wrongly rejected while accepting the nonexistent REFO. |
37	| LFMODCLK | MODCLK through a fixed, non-configurable /128 → 37.5 kHz (SLAU367P §3.2.5). Coded as the relationship `MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ / 128`, not a second literal. The only crystal-free low-frequency ACLK source besides VLO; LFMODCLK/8 reports 4688 (4687.5 rounded by `:.0f`). |
38	| DCO | The digitally controlled oscillator: tunable (`clock.dco_frequency`, default 1e6) and drift-affected (`_dco_actual()` = setting × `dco_factor()`, ±3.5% CORNER). Reset-default source for MCLK/SMCLK — and the only branch of `_clock_source_frequency()` that carries drift. |
39	| derived-value query | A query answered by computing from the governing configuration chain at read time (resolve source → base frequency → apply divider), never from a cache or a default. The old `CLOCK:*:FREQUENCY?` always read DCO/LFXT — stored, echoed, never consulted — the bug class 701853d fixed. |
40	| PxREN | The MSP430 per-port pull-resistor-enable register (SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1): one bit per pin connects a weak resistor; the pin's PxOUT bit selects the direction (0=pulldown, 1=pullup). Modeled as the stored `resistor_enable` field, exposed via `GPIO:PORTn:RESISTOR:ENABLE` (`_gpio_ren`). |
41	| register repurposing | One register bit meaning different things depending on other state — PxOUT is the drive level when PxDIR=1 but the pull-direction select when PxDIR=0 and PxREN=1 (cf. TAxCCRn under the CAP bit). The model must store the documented registers and derive meanings, not one storage per meaning. |
42	| inexpressible state | A simulator state no register-write sequence can produce on the real part, e.g. both pulls active on one pin under the old independent masks (`probe_gpio_pull_both`). Tests passing there certify nothing; the fix makes it unrepresentable — `pullup & pulldown == 0` by construction. |
43	| derived view | A value computed at read time from stored registers instead of stored itself: `pullup = REN & OUT & 0xFF`, `pulldown = REN & ~OUT & 0xFF` as read-only `@property`s on `GPIOPort`. Cannot desynchronise from its sources; the `& 0xFF` clamps Python's unbounded `~` to the port's 8 lines. |
44	| deprecated alias | A kept-for-compatibility command that owns no state and composes the real registers: `GPIO:PORTn:PULLUP m` does `REN \|= m; OUT \|= m`, PULLDOWN does `REN \|= m; OUT &= ~m`; queries return the derived views. Old scripts keep working, impossible states stay impossible. |
45	| pull-up / pull-down | A weak resistor tying an undriven input pin to VCC (reads 1) or GND (reads 0) so it doesn't float. On MSP430 mutually exclusive per pin: one PxREN enable, one PxOUT direction bit — `RESISTOR:ENABLE 0xFF` + `OUTPUT 0xFF` makes an all-input port read `0xFF`. |
46	| undriven pin | An input pin nobody drives. With REN clear it reads the injected value (floats on hardware); with REN set, `_gpio_inp` returns PxOUT's bit — the pull level — and masks injection out (`& ~resistor_enable`): no drive-strength model, so simulating an external override means clearing REN first. |
47	| single source of truth (registers) | Storing exactly the documented registers (`direction`, `output`, `input`, `resistor_enable`) once each and deriving every other representation, so one write updates all views and no two copies can disagree — the same discipline as the PERIOD→TAxCCR0 aliasing fix. |
48	| MSP430X / CPUX | TI's extended MSP430 CPU (SLAU367P §4.3): R0–R15 widened to 20 bits and the address space to 1 MB while 16-bit instruction encodings run unchanged. `_cpu_reg` now masks writes with `& 0xFFFFF`; the old `& 0xFFFF` modelled the wrong CPU. |
49	| 20-bit register | A register with 20 physical flip-flops (max 0xFFFFF = 1,048,575); bits 19:16 select one of sixteen 64-KB pages. `probe_cpu_reg_20bit` pins the round trip: write 0x12345, read back `"0x12345"` — the old 16-bit mask returned `"0x2345"` with no error. |

# Silmulator — Glossary

Terms the learner has demonstrably grasped are added here.

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| ConnectionPort | A `QGraphicsEllipseItem` child of a block that holds `port_id`, `parent_block`, and `connected_to` (the peer port, or None). Coloured blue when free, green when connected. |
| WireItem | A `QGraphicsLineItem` in the scene (not a child of any block) that draws a gold line between two ConnectionPorts. ZValue = -1 so blocks render above it. |
| x_frac / y_frac | Fractional coordinates (0.0–1.0) passed to `add_port()` that are multiplied by the block's BLOCK_WIDTH / BLOCK_HEIGHT to position a port in local coordinates. |
| hardware_docs/ | The folder in the repo where vendor PDFs, SCPI command tables, and notes are stored. Not auto-parsed; feeds the custom-block authoring workflow. |
| custom block spec | A JSON file in `silmulator/custom_blocks/` that declares a block's name, colour, port layout, and SCPI command map. Loaded at startup by `discover_specs()`. |
| SIL | Software-in-the-Loop: both the controller logic and the instruments are simulated in software. No real hardware. |
| HIL | Hardware-in-the-Loop: the real embedded controller runs in real time; only the instruments/plant are simulated. |
| CIL | Code-in-the-Loop: actual source files are the artifact under test; SCPI calls extracted from them are replayed against simulated instruments. The Code Input block enables this. |
| SCPI | Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (IEEE 488.2). A tree-structured text command language used by lab instruments and simulated here. |
| reference voltage | The voltage pair (VR+/VR−) an ADC compares its input against — the conversion's unit of measure. In the MSP430 model, `_adc_reference_voltage()` resolves VR+ from the selected `ADC:REFERENCE` (AVCC live via `clock.vcc`, REF_A outputs, or VeREF+); VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V). |
| full-scale code | The maximum ADC output, 2^resolution − 1 (4095/1023/255). Produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage. Clamped in `FaultState.adc_code()`. |
| transfer function | The input→code mapping NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−)/(VR+ − VR−) (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13). An ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage. Implemented as `int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)`, clamped. |
| LSB voltage | The input-voltage width of one code step: (VR+ − VR−)/FS. ≈293 µV under the 1.2-V VREF vs ≈806 µV under 3.3-V AVCC at 12 bits — the reference sets granularity as well as range. |

Why this matters: converging tonight's six-branch stack made docs/learning/PROGRESS.md collide twice — once loudly (a conflict block at 24f142b) and once silently (a clean auto-merge at f2b6fbf that produced two "Session 4" headings). Git merges lines, not meaning: an append-only log conflicts at its append anchor by construction, and a merge that satisfies git can still violate the file's invariants.

☐ 3. The real conflict
☐ 4. Keep-one vs keep-both
☐ 5. The silent bad merge
☐ 6. Derived files
☐ 7. Merge vs rebase
☐ 8. Verification
☐ 9. Misconceptions
☐ 10. Quiz

1. Three-Way Merge Mechanics: Base, Ours, Theirs

git merge never compares two files. It compares three versions of each file:

  • Base — the file at the merge base, the nearest common ancestor of the two branches. Tonight: git merge-base 24f142b^1 24f142b^2 → df5c43c, the last commit both histories share.
  • Ours — the file on the branch you are standing on (HEAD, the first parent of the merge).
  • Theirs — the file on the branch being merged in (the second parent).

The base is what makes the merge three-way, and it is the whole trick: by diffing each side against the base, git learns who changed what, not just how the two sides differ. The decision rule is applied region by region:

BaseOursTheirsResult
AAAA — nobody changed it
ABAB — only ours changed it, take ours
AABB — only theirs changed it, take theirs
ABBB — both made the identical change
ABCCONFLICT — both changed the same region differently
(nothing)B insertedC insertedCONFLICT — both inserted at the same point; git has no ordering rule

Two properties of this algorithm drive everything in this lesson:

  • It is line-based and content-agnostic. Git does not know a session log from a C file. Its unit of change is the line; its notion of "the same place" is the surrounding unchanged context lines. It has no idea what a "Session number" is, so it cannot know that two different lines both saying ### Session 3 are a problem — or that two non-colliding edits can add up to one.
  • A conflict is a refusal, not an error. The bottom two rows are the cases where any automatic choice would be a guess. Git stops, writes both candidates into the file between markers, and makes a human (or tonight, an agent) decide. Everything it can decide from the table above, it decides silently — which is where Section 5's trouble comes from.
📌 Reading a merge commit
A merge commit has two parents: git show 24f142b prints Merge: 19d2688 d63bbbf. When you commit a resolved conflict, git records the conflicted paths in the default message — 24f142b's message carries # Conflicts: Silmulator/docs/learning/PROGRESS.md, and f2b6fbf's carries only index.html. That trailer is tonight's documentary evidence of which collision was loud and which was silent.

2. Why Append-Only Logs Conflict by Construction

PROGRESS.md is an append-only log: every overnight session appends one ### Session N block at the same structural position — after the last existing entry, immediately before the ## Suggested Next Lessons tail. That position is the file's append anchor: the pair of stable context lines every writer inserts between.

### Drill 1 (2026-06-20)          ← last shared entry (context above)
…entry body…
                                  ← every new session is inserted HERE
## Suggested Next Lessons         ← stable tail (context below)

Now run the three-way rule from Section 1 over two branches that each logged a session. Both diffs against the base say the same thing: "insert lines between the Drill 1 block and the Suggested heading." Same context above, same context below, different inserted content — that is the bottom row of the table. Conflict, by construction.

This is the key contrast with source code. Two branches editing msp430.py usually touch different functions, so their hunks have different context and merge cleanly. Two branches appending to a log always touch the same anchor. For a shared append-only file, conflict is not bad luck or bad manners — it is the steady state of parallel work. The same shape applies to CHANGELOGs, migration lists, and this repo's GLOSSARY.md (append-at-end table) and PROGRESS.md.

Three standard mitigations: (1) one file per entry — changelog fragments in a directory (changelog.d/, "towncrier" style), assembled at release time, so parallel entries are parallel files and never collide; (2) a union merge driver (.gitattributes: merge=union) that keeps both sides automatically — but see Section 9 for why that is a trap for numbered logs; (3) accept the conflict and repair the invariants by hand — this repo's choice, viable because sessions are infrequent and the invariants are easy to assert. Note that choice (1) is exactly the shape of lessons/ + the generated index.html: per-entry files plus a derived aggregate.
⚠ The anchor moves with the content
"Append-only" describes the discipline, not a magic file mode. The moment one branch also renames an old heading (as the 24f142b resolution renamed Session 3 → Session 4), its diff is no longer a pure insertion at the anchor — and that is precisely what lets a later merge slide past the anchor without conflicting. Section 5 is the case study.

7. Merge vs Rebase When SHAs Are Shared

The alternative at 24f142b would have been git rebase origin/master: replay the feature branch's commits on top of master and get a straight line instead of a join. Rebase has real virtues — but it rewrites every replayed commit, giving each a new SHA. For tonight's stack that cost is disqualifying, because the old SHAs are cited in prose:

  • PROGRESS.md itself: "Grounded in commit 58b7e2d", "a20fbb1", "701853d", "4cb71a1", "07f1f69"…
  • Lesson headers: lesson 0009's label reads "from issue #18, commit 58b7e2d"; its quiz answers reference the commit by SHA.

Rebase the branch and every one of those citations dangles: the text still says 58b7e2d, but that commit no longer belongs to any branch's history (it survives only until garbage collection), and after the force-push the SHA-links in PR discussions point at orphans. A reader clicking through from the lesson finds nothing. Merging preserves every existing SHA immutably and adds one new join commit; the conflict is resolved once, in that commit, and the resolution is itself recorded history (git show 24f142b shows exactly what the resolver chose).

Three-Way Merge Semantics — Vocabulary

Eight terms behind tonight's two PROGRESS.md collisions — one loud, one silent. Each has a definition, a project example from the real merge history, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

three-way merge merge base conflict hunk keep-both resolution semantic invariant append anchor derived file merge-tree dry run

Three-way merge

base + ours + theirs → result
Definition
The merge algorithm that combines two versions of a file by consulting a third — their common ancestor. Diffing each side against the base reveals who changed what; regions changed by only one side are taken automatically, identical changes are taken once, and regions changed differently by both sides become conflicts. It is line-based and content-agnostic: git merges text regions, never meanings.
Project example
Commit 24f142b merged origin/master into feature/issue-18-adc-reference-scaling. For PROGRESS.md the three inputs were base df5c43c (no Session 3 at all), ours (Session 3 = the July ADC entry), theirs (Session 3 = the June visual-testing entry). Both sides inserted at the same point → one conflict hunk. Reproducible offline: git merge-file -p --diff3 ours.md base.md theirs.md.
Usage
"Don't reason from the two branch tips alone — a three-way merge decides by each side's diff against the base, so look at what each branch changed, not how they differ."
Contrast with: two-way diff/merge
A two-way comparison sees only that the sides differ, not who diverged from what — every difference looks like a coin-flip. The base turns "these differ" into "ours added X, theirs added Y", which is what makes automatic merging (and the keep-both diagnosis) possible at all.

Merge base

git merge-base A B — the nearest common ancestor
Definition
The most recent commit reachable from both branches — the point where their histories diverged, and the "base" input of the three-way merge. Everything after it on either side is that side's contribution; the choice of base therefore decides what counts as "changed".
Project example
git merge-base 24f142b^1 24f142b^2 → df5c43c, whose log ends at Drill 1 — proving neither Session 3 existed before the fork and both were insertions. The later convergence merge f2b6fbf had a different base, 701853d, where the ADC entry already existed as Session 3 — which is why theirs' rename of that heading registered as a change and merged silently with ours' appends.
Usage
"Before merging, run git log $(git merge-base HEAD origin/master)..origin/master -- PROGRESS.md — everything it lists is what 'theirs' will bring to the table."
Contrast with: branch point you remember
After prior merges, the merge base moves: because 24f142b merged master in, later merges use a much newer base than the original fork. The base is computed from the graph (lowest common ancestor), not from team folklore about "where we branched".

Conflict hunk

<<<<<<< ours ======= theirs >>>>>>>
Definition
The disputed region git writes into the working file when both sides changed the same region differently: ours' candidate above the ======= separator, theirs' below, delimited by the <<<<<<</>>>>>>> markers (plus the base text under ||||||| in diff3 style). It is a question, not an error — resolving means replacing the entire hunk, markers included, with the final text.
Project example
The single hunk at 24f142b sat at PROGRESS.md's append anchor: ours' July "Session 3 (…issue #18)" block above the separator, theirs' June "Session 3 (2026-06-28, overnight)" block below, and — under diff3 — an empty base section, the fingerprint of both-sides-append. The resolution replaced the hunk with both entries, June first, July renumbered to Session 4.
Usage
"Read the whole hunk before touching it — the dates and issue numbers inside it are the evidence for the keep-one vs keep-both diagnosis."
Contrast with: conflict markers
The markers are just the delimiters; the hunk is the content between them. Deleting the markers without merging the content (or missing one — a stray =======) "resolves" nothing: the post-merge sweep greps for anchored, length-exact marker lines precisely because git will happily commit leftovers.

Keep-both resolution

two events → two records
Definition
Resolving a conflict by including both sides' text — the correct outcome when the hunk holds two records of different events rather than two versions of one record. The kept entries are ordered by the file's own rule (not by git's ours-first layout), and any invariants that keeping both breaks (duplicate numbering) are repaired as part of the resolution.
Project example
24f142b kept master's June visual-testing entry and the branch's July ADC entry: different dates, different issues, and the merge itself brought lesson 0008's files into the tree — dropping either entry would make the log deny work the tree contains. June stayed Session 3; July was renumbered to Session 4.
Usage
"Both sides appended and the diff3 base is empty — that's a keep-both: take both entries, chronological order, and renumber the later one."
Contrast with: --ours / --theirs (keep-one)
Keep-one is right when the sides are two versions of the same record (keep the revision or the superset). Applied to a both-sides-append log it silently deletes one branch's true history — the one-keystroke "resolution" that recreates exactly the data loss the conflict existed to prevent.

Semantic invariant

the file's rules that git cannot see
Definition
A property a file must satisfy that lives above the line level — unique IDs, monotonic numbering, chronological order, exactly one tail section. Line-based tools can produce output that is textually consistent with both parents yet violates these rules: textual success is not semantic success.
Project example
PROGRESS.md's invariants: session numbers unique and monotonically increasing, entries chronological, one ## Suggested Next Lessons tail. The f2b6fbf auto-merge (exit 0, zero markers) violated the first two — a duplicate ### Session 4 and an off-by-one tail — because ours' appended numbering was premised on an assumption theirs' renumbering had invalidated. Repair: renumber five headings, then assert grep -oE '^### Session [0-9]+' | sort | uniq -d prints nothing.
Usage
"The merge was clean, but run the invariant checks anyway — clean only means git had no questions, not that the answers were right."
Contrast with: textual conflict
A textual conflict is loud — git stops and demands a decision. An invariant violation after a clean merge is silent — no message, no marker, wrong file. The loud failure is the safe one; the guard (pre-commit/CI assertion) exists for the silent one.

Append anchor

where every writer inserts
Definition
The stable context lines between which an append-only file receives every new entry — end of the last record above, fixed tail below. Because all writers insert between the same context, any two branches that both appended have changed "the same region": append-only logs conflict at the anchor by construction, not by accident.
Project example
PROGRESS.md's anchor is the gap between the last session block and ## Suggested Next Lessons. Master and the issue-18 branch each inserted a Session 3 there → the 24f142b conflict. Same shape: GLOSSARY.md (append-at-end table). The mitigation spectrum: per-entry files (as lessons/ does), a union merge driver (dangerous), or accept-and-repair (this repo's choice).
Usage
"Two overnight branches both logged sessions, so expect a conflict at the append anchor — that's the file working as designed, not someone's mistake."
Contrast with: ordinary code-edit collision
Source-code conflicts require the bad luck of touching the same lines; parallel work usually lands in different functions and merges cleanly. The anchor removes the luck: every append targets the same spot, so collision probability is ~100% per pair of appending branches. Also note the anchor only guards pure appends — once a side edits old headings too (the Session-3→4 rename), changes can slide past it silently (f2b6fbf).

Derived file

regenerate, don't merge
Definition
A file that is a deterministic projection of other sources — an index, lockfile, generated report, build output. It is not a source of truth, so merging it hunk-by-hunk answers the wrong question: the correct "resolution" of any conflict in it is to resolve the sources, then rerun the generator.
Project example
docs/learning/index.html hit an add/add conflict at f2b6fbf: absent at base 701853d, created independently on both sides (43 vs 54 lines, even disagreeing on doctype casing). Resolution: take neither; run python3 docs/learning/.tools/build_index.py against the merged directory. The regenerated 44-line file matches neither parent and indexes the union — more correct than both.
Usage
"That's a generated index under conflict — don't pick a side, rebuild it after the lesson files land; that's also why tonight's session doesn't touch index.html."
Contrast with: source of truth
The test: "if I deleted this file, could one command recreate it?" Yes → derived; the command is the resolution. No → source of truth (PROGRESS.md, lesson HTML, Python code); merge it and resolve conflicts by diagnosis. Hand-merging derived output can, at absolute best, slowly imitate the generator.

Merge-tree dry run

git merge-tree — predict conflicts without touching anything
Definition
An in-memory merge that reports what git merge would do — conflicted paths and result tree — without moving HEAD, changing the working tree, or requiring it to be clean. Modern form: git merge-tree --write-tree ours theirs (git ≥ 2.38, nonzero exit on conflict); classic form: git merge-tree base ours theirs, which prints the would-be hunks.
Project example
Before converging tonight's stack, git merge-tree --write-tree --no-messages HEAD origin/master would have predicted the PROGRESS.md conflict at 24f142b in milliseconds — and its silence about PROGRESS.md before f2b6fbf is itself information: "this file will merge cleanly, so schedule the invariant check instead of a resolution."
Usage
"Dry-run the merge first — if merge-tree lists PROGRESS.md, plan the keep-both resolution before you start, not in the middle of a half-merged tree."
Contrast with: git merge --no-commit / merge-and-abort
A real merge with --no-commit mutates the index and working tree and demands a clean state; --abort must then unwind it. merge-tree is pure computation on the object database — safe to run mid-work, in scripts, or in CI, and the natural first step of an overnight agent's convergence plan.
